title.en: RAG architecture and when not to use RAG

body.en:
**In this lesson you will learn:**

- 1) How Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems are architected end-to-end: ingestion, chunking, embeddings, indexing, retrieval, reranking, prompting, generation, and post-processing.
- 2) How to select retrieval techniques (sparse, dense, hybrid), vector stores, metadata filtering, and caching to balance quality, latency, and cost.
- 3) When not to use RAG, including tasks better served by structured queries, deterministic pipelines, fine-tuning, or where latency, privacy, or governance constraints preclude retrieval.

blocks.title: Learn RAG From Scratch – Python AI Tutorial from a LangChain Engineer
blocks.label: Course Video

objectiveBefore.fr: Pendant cette vidéo, repérez les éléments qui illustrent « What You Will Learn » avant de poursuivre.
objectiveBefore.en: While watching, identify the elements that illustrate “What You Will Learn” before continuing.

body.en:
RAG augments an LLM with up-to-date, task-relevant context retrieved from external knowledge sources at query time.

The pipeline typically includes: (1) Ingestion: collect sources (files, web, databases), normalize, deduplicate, and apply text extraction and cleaning.

(2) Chunking: split documents into semantically coherent segments with overlap to preserve context; attach metadata (source, author, timestamp, ACL, schema).

(3) Embeddings and Indexing: create vector representations and store alongside sparse indexes (BM25) to enable hybrid retrieval; add filters on metadata (time, type, tenant).

(4) Retrieval: route the query (optionally expanded or rewritten) to the index, retrieve top-k candidates, and apply a cross-encoder reranker to improve precision.

(5) Prompt Assembly: format citations and snippets into a templated prompt; constrain length and deduplicate.

(6) Generation: have the LLM answer grounded in retrieved context, optionally with tool use (e.g., calculators, SQL) and guardrails.

(7) Post-processing: cite sources, red-team checks, PII scrubbing, and caching of results.

Architectural choices trade off quality, latency, and cost: hybrid search often improves recall; reranking boosts precision; smaller chunk sizes help localization but can lose context; larger chunks increase recall but risk dilution.

Evaluate with retrieval metrics (recall@k, MRR), answer metrics (faithfulness, exact match, factuality), latency SLOs, and cost per query.

Avoid RAG when: the task is deterministic or purely structured (e.g., SQL lookups or rules-based extraction); the domain is narrow and stable where fine-tuning a small model is cheaper and faster; strict offline or ultra-low latency constraints make retrieval infeasible; or governance disallows exposing or transporting sensitive data into prompts even with filtering.

In such cases, alternatives include direct database queries, search-only UX, fine-tuning, or knowledge distillation into smaller models.

• Retrieval strategies: Sparse (BM25), dense (vector), and hybrid retrieval; query rewriting and expansion to improve recall.
• Index and chunk design: Semantic chunking with overlap, rich metadata, and embeddings to balance context with precision.
• When not to use RAG: Prefer structured queries, deterministic pipelines, or fine-tuning when data is stable, outputs must be exact, or latency/governance constraints block retrieval.

• RAG augments LLMs with retrieved, cited context to improve factuality and freshness.
• Architectural choices (hybrid retrieval, chunking, reranking, caching) control the quality-latency-cost trade-offs.
• Avoid RAG for deterministic, structured, or highly constrained tasks where databases, rules, or fine-tuning are superior.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand the core concepts and can apply them in practice.

title.en: Source inventory, data ownership, freshness and ACL

body.en:
**In this lesson you will learn:**

- 1) How to build a comprehensive source inventory with ownership, lineage, sensitivity, and SLAs.
- 2) How to design freshness pipelines using CDC, incremental indexing, versioning, and invalidation to keep RAG up to date.
- 3) How to enforce access control with per-tenant partitioning, per-chunk ACL metadata, retrieval-time filtering, and auditable access.

A source inventory catalogs every data source feeding RAG: system name, owner (team and on-call), data steward, schema, formats, update frequency, SLAs, sensitivity (PII/PHI/secret), retention, and lineage.

Clear ownership enables governance, escalation, and change management.

Data freshness requires aligning ingest and indexing with source change patterns.

Prefer event-driven pipelines using change data capture (CDC), webhooks, or message queues to perform incremental updates (upserts/deletes) rather than full reindexing.

Track document IDs, versions, and timestamps; implement invalidation hooks so outdated chunks are removed or replaced atomically.

For large sources, use batching with backpressure, and apply deduplication, canonicalization, and quality checks (e.g., checksum drift, schema validation).

Access control must prevent unauthorized context from entering prompts.

Attach ACL metadata (tenant, group, user, labels) to each document/chunk and enforce filtering at retrieval using the caller’s entitlements.

Combine with index partitioning per tenant when isolation is required; for multi-tenant shared indexes, always filter on ACL metadata and avoid mixing unauthorized chunks in the prompt.

Secure blob storage with signed URLs or KMS keys, and log/audit retrievals.

Apply row/segment-level security where feasible, and ensure caches are scoped by identity and ACL.

Regularly test ACLs with synthetic queries and red-team probes to prevent leakage.

Finally, maintain data lifecycle policies (retention, legal hold) and monitor freshness (lag, staleness rate) and coverage (% of eligible sources indexed).

title.en: Parsing PDFs, HTML, Markdown, CSV and structured records

body.en:
**In this lesson you will learn:**

- 1) How to select and configure robust parsers for PDFs, HTML, Markdown, CSV, and structured records (e.g., JSON/Parquet)
- 2) How to preserve and normalize structure (headings, tables, links, code, reading order) into chunkable text with reliable citations
- 3) How to handle quality issues (OCR for scans, encoding, line wraps) and attach source-aware metadata for effective RAG retrieval.

Reliable RAG pipelines start with faithful parsing that preserves semantics and provenance.

For PDFs, prefer native text extraction (e.g., PDFMiner/PyMuPDF) and fall back to OCR for scanned pages; fix issues like broken line wraps, hyphenation, and detect reading order; extract tables with table-aware tools (e.g., Camelot/Tabula) and keep page numbers and bounding boxes for citations.

HTML should be parsed via the DOM, stripping boilerplate (nav/ads) and retaining semantic blocks (h1–h6, p, li, table, code, figure); resolve relative links, capture anchors, and normalize whitespace; chunk by headings or DOM boundaries.

Markdown should be parsed with an AST to preserve headings, lists, code fences, and tables; convert to normalized plain text while keeping structure markers for later chunking.

CSV and record-oriented data (JSON, Parquet) should be read with schema-aware libraries to preserve types, headers, and nulls; treat rows or logical groups as records and avoid lossy stringification.

Across formats, normalize encodings (UTF-8), unify newline conventions, and attach source metadata (source_uri, page or section path, mime_type, checksum) at both document and chunk levels.

Chunking strategies should respect natural boundaries (pages, headings, list items, table rows) and target token budgets while maintaining context for accurate grounding and citations.

• Format-aware extraction: Use parsers that understand layout and semantics for each file type.
• Structure-preserving normalization: Keep headings, tables, links, code blocks, and reading order before chunking.
• Provenance metadata: Attach source_uri, page/anchor, mime_type, checksums, and parser/ocr details to each chunk.

• Use format-specific parsers and hybrid OCR strategies to maximize fidelity.
• Normalize and chunk along semantic boundaries while retaining structure and citations.
• Attach rich, consistent metadata (source, section/page, types) at document and chunk levels.

title.en: Metadata design for citations and filtering

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) How to design a metadata schema that supports trustworthy citations and precise filtering 2) How to capture provenance, structure, and access control at both document and chunk levels 3) How to implement consistent typing, normalization, and indexing across vector and keyword stores for scalable RAG.

Effective metadata enables grounding (citations) and control (filtering).

At minimum, include identifiers (doc_id, chunk_id, chunk_index), source fields (source_uri, mime_type, checksum/hash/etag), structural locators (page, html_anchor, section_path, span_offsets), and timestamps (created_at, updated_at, valid_from/valid_to).

Provenance should track pipeline_version, extractor/ocr details, embedding_model/version, and quality/confidence.

Distinguish document-level fields (authors, title, canonical_source, language, ACL defaults) from chunk-level fields (page/section, chunk_index, local offsets, entities).

For filtering, define type-safe facets such as product, region, environment, version, tags, language, and access controls (tenant_id, allowed_groups/roles, sensitivity/classification).

Normalize value types (string, int, bool, datetime, array) and avoid free-form comma-separated strings.

Ensure your vector database supports filtering on these fields; if not, maintain a synchronized keyword/relational index for complex filters and join on ids.

For citations, store precise anchors (page numbers, HTML ids/XPaths, character offsets) so UIs can generate clickable references and highlights.

Use namespaces or an embedding_version field to prevent mixing vectors across model upgrades.

Finally, document the schema, enforce it in ingestion, and validate at write time to keep metadata consistent over time.

• Citation metadata: doc_id/source_uri with page or anchor plus span_offsets enable accurate, clickable references.
• Filter facets and ACLs: type-safe fields (tenant_id, roles, region, product, dates) support precise, auditable retrieval scopes.
• Versioning and provenance: embedding_version, pipeline_version, checksum, and confidence enable deduplication, rollbacks, and quality control.

• Separate document-level and chunk-level metadata and enforce consistent types.
• Store precise citation anchors (page/anchor/offsets) and provenance for trustworthy answers.
• Design filterable facets and ACLs; version embeddings and pipelines to manage change safely.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand the core concepts and can apply them in practice.

Chunking is the process of splitting documents into smaller units before embedding and indexing. The strategy chosen directly impacts retrieval accuracy.

**Fixed chunking** splits text into equal-size windows (e.g., 512 tokens) with optional overlap. It is simple and fast but ignores semantic boundaries, often cutting sentences mid-thought.

**Semantic chunking** groups sentences or paragraphs by topic similarity using embedding cosine distance. It preserves meaning but is computationally heavier.

**Recursive chunking** applies a hierarchy of separators (paragraphs → sentences → words) until chunks reach the target size. It respects natural language structure better than fixed splitting.

**Document-aware chunking** leverages the document's own structure — headings, sections, tables, and metadata — to define chunk boundaries. It is ideal for structured formats like PDFs, HTML, and Markdown, ensuring that each chunk is semantically self-contained and contextually meaningful.

body.en:
An embedding model converts text into dense numerical vectors that capture semantic meaning. Selecting the right model is critical for retrieval quality.

**Key selection criteria** include: context window size (how many tokens can be embedded at once), output dimensionality (higher dimensions capture more nuance but increase storage and compute), and benchmark scores such as MTEB (Massive Text Embedding Benchmark).

Popular models include OpenAI's text-embedding-3-large, Cohere Embed v3, and open-source options like BGE-M3 and E5-mistral. Each offers different cost, latency, and accuracy trade-offs.

**Multilingual embeddings** such as multilingual-e5-large, LaBSE, and BGE-M3 encode text from dozens of languages into a shared vector space, enabling cross-lingual retrieval. This is essential for global applications where documents and queries may be in different languages.

A critical rule is **embedding symmetry**: the same model must be used at both index time and query time. Mixing models invalidates the vector space and produces incorrect similarity scores.

Maintaining a clean vector index is as important as the embedding model itself. Dirty data leads to redundant retrieval results, inflated index sizes, and degraded generation quality.

**Normalization** standardizes text before embedding: lowercasing, whitespace trimming, Unicode normalization (NFC/NFKC), removal of boilerplate headers and footers, and HTML tag stripping. Consistent normalization ensures that semantically identical text produces consistent embeddings.

**Content hashing** assigns a deterministic fingerprint (e.g., SHA-256 or MD5) to each chunk's text after normalization. Before indexing, the pipeline checks whether a hash already exists in the store. If it does, the chunk is skipped, preventing exact duplicates from inflating the index.

**Near-duplicate detection** goes further, using techniques like MinHash or SimHash to find chunks that are highly similar but not byte-identical. These are common when documents share boilerplate sections or when multiple versions of the same document are ingested. Removing near-duplicates improves retrieval diversity and reduces noise in the context window passed to the language model.

In production RAG systems, source documents are rarely static. Incremental indexing ensures that your vector store reflects the current state of your corpus without requiring expensive full re-indexing operations.

**Incremental indexing** processes only new or modified documents since the last indexing run. It relies on change detection mechanisms: comparing document modification timestamps, file checksums, or content hashes against records stored in a metadata catalog.

**Re-index triggers** are events that signal the need to update the index. Common triggers include: a document's last-modified timestamp changing, a content hash mismatch indicating that the document body has changed, a new document being added to the source, a document being deleted (requiring vector removal), or a change in the chunking strategy or embedding model (requiring full re-indexing).

**Index drift** occurs when the vector store diverges from the source of truth over time. This manifests as stale vectors pointing to outdated content, missing vectors for new documents, and orphaned vectors for deleted documents. A well-designed incremental pipeline must handle all three cases: upsert for new and modified chunks, and delete for removed ones. Scheduled audits comparing source document inventories against indexed vector IDs help detect and remediate drift.

title.en: Vector search basics: cosine, dot product, HNSW, IVF

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) How cosine similarity, dot product, and Euclidean distance differ and when to use each 2) How HNSW and IVF accelerate nearest neighbor search and the key tuning parameters 3) How to reason about recall vs. latency trade-offs and evaluate ANN quality

body.en:
Vector search retrieves items by comparing high-dimensional embeddings. Common metrics: Euclidean (L2) distance, cosine distance (1 − cosine similarity), and inner product (dot product). For L2-normalized vectors, cosine similarity and dot product induce the same ranking; without normalization, dot product favors larger-norm vectors.

Approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) indexes trade a small, controllable loss in recall for large latency reductions vs. brute-force search. HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) builds a multi-layer small-world graph. Search starts at the top layer and descends, expanding a candidate set controlled by ef_search. Key parameters: M (graph degree, higher increases recall/memory), ef_construction (larger improves recall/build time), ef_search (larger improves recall/query time). HNSW supports fast incremental inserts and high recall at low latency.

IVF (Inverted File) partitions vectors via a coarse quantizer (e.g., k-means) into 'lists' (centroids). At query time, only the closest lists (nprobe) are scanned; within lists, exact (IVF-Flat) or compressed (e.g., PQ/OPQ in some systems) distances are computed. Tuning lists balances index granularity; nprobe balances recall vs. speed. IVF typically prefers bulk training on data and is efficient for batch-oriented workloads.

Evaluation focuses on recall@k (vs. exact search), latency (P50/P95), memory, and build time. Metric choice must align with the embedding model and task: cosine for semantic similarity with normalized embeddings, L2 for geometry-preserving spaces, inner product for models trained with margin-based objectives. Filters and metadata constraints can be handled by pre-filtering candidates, post-filter re-ranking, or index partitioning.

• Metric selection: Cosine vs. dot product vs. L2; normalization changes ranking behavior
• HNSW trade-offs: M/ef_construction/ef_search tune memory, build time, recall, and latency
• IVF trade-offs: lists (coarse partitions) and nprobe (lists searched) control recall/speed

• Choose a metric that matches your model and normalize when appropriate
• HNSW excels at high-recall, low-latency search with live inserts
• IVF trades accuracy for speed via lists and nprobe; tune them to balance recall and latency
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand the core concepts and can apply them in practice.

title.en: pgvector in Postgres for small-to-medium RAG

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) How to install pgvector, model schemas, and store embeddings in Postgres 2) How to choose metrics and create IVFFlat/HNSW indexes with the right parameters 3) How to run kNN and hybrid (keyword + vector) queries for effective RAG

pgvector adds a vector data type and kNN indexing to Postgres, making it practical for small-to-medium RAG systems that benefit from SQL, transactions, and unified storage.

Setup and schema: CREATE EXTENSION pgvector; define columns as vector(d), where d matches your embedding dimension (e.g., 384, 768, 1536). Example: CREATE TABLE docs (id bigserial PRIMARY KEY, content text, meta jsonb, embedding vector(768)); Insert embeddings from your application using parameter binding and cast (e.g., $1::vector).

Similarity operators and opclasses: <-> computes L2 distance, <#> computes inner product, <=> computes cosine distance. Choose a matching operator class for indexes: vector_l2_ops, vector_ip_ops, or vector_cosine_ops. Query with ORDER BY embedding <-> $1::vector (or <#>, <=>) LIMIT k.

Indexes: Two common ANN indexes are IVFFlat and HNSW. IVFFlat partitions data into lists and scans nprobe lists at query time. Build after bulk-loading data so the quantizer can train well: CREATE INDEX docs_embedding_ivf ON docs USING ivfflat (embedding vector_cosine_ops) WITH (lists = 100); Tune per-query with SET ivfflat.probes = 10; higher probes improves recall. HNSW supports incremental inserts and strong recall: CREATE INDEX docs_embedding_hnsw ON docs USING hnsw (embedding vector_l2_ops) WITH (m = 16, ef_construction = 200); Tune search with SET hnsw.ef_search = 80; higher values increase recall and latency.

Hybrid retrieval: Combine Postgres full-text search with vector search. Create a tsvector column (generated or materialized) and GIN index for text: to_tsvector('english', content). You can rank by (a) two-stage retrieval (vector kNN -> filter/rerank with text or vice versa), (b) weighted scoring (e.g., ts_rank * wt_text − distance * wt_vec), or (c) rank fusion like RRF: 1/(k + rank). Example pattern: get top-N by text and top-N by vector in CTEs, UNION ALL, then aggregate by id with SUM of RRF scores.

Operational notes: ANALYZE after loading to help planners; keep dimensions consistent; choose cosine for normalized embeddings; monitor P95 latency and recall@k vs. exact scan to validate quality. For small-to-medium deployments (e.g., up to a few million embeddings on a single node), pgvector offers good performance; beyond that, consider sharding or specialized vector stores.

title.en: Qdrant for dedicated vector search and payload filtering

body.en:
**In this lesson you will learn:**

- 1) How Qdrant organizes collections, vectors, and payloads to deliver fast ANN search with precise server-side filtering.
- 2) How to model data using named vectors and payload schemas, and when to add payload indexes for high-cardinality filters.
- 3) How to design performant queries with must/should/must_not filters, range and geo constraints, score thresholds, and HNSW search parameters for accuracy and throughput.

Qdrant is a vector database optimized for approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search with rich, server-side payload filtering. Data lives in collections that hold points. Each point stores one or more vectors and an associated payload (structured metadata). Qdrant’s ANN engine is built on HNSW graphs, where ef (size of the candidate list at query time) trades latency for recall, and m/ef_construct control index build quality and memory. Distance metrics (Cosine, Dot, Euclidean) determine how similarity is scored.

Payload filtering allows you to constrain vector search results by metadata without additional application-side joins. Filters support boolean logic via must, should, and must_not; field matches (exact or any-of), numeric ranges (gt/gte/lt/lte), existence checks, geo filters (radius or bounding box on lat/lon fields), and ID-based selection. For high-selectivity queries at scale, you can create payload indexes to accelerate filters (e.g., keyword, integer/float, and geo). Proper indexing avoids scanning large payloads during ANN.

Qdrant supports named vectors so a single point can carry multiple embeddings (e.g., title and body), each with its own distance metric and search params. You can choose between storing vectors fully in RAM or enabling on-disk optimizations; optional quantization can reduce memory at some accuracy cost. Query design typically combines a vector, a filter (e.g., tenant_id, doc_type, time range), a limit/top-k, and parameters like ef and score_threshold. Good practice: index frequently-filtered fields, keep filters selective but not overly narrow, and tune ef to recover recall when filters shrink the candidate set.

• HNSW search parameters: ef improves recall at higher latency; distance metric shapes scoring.
• Payload filtering: must/should/must_not logic with match, range, exists, and geo constraints executed server-side.
• Data modeling: use named vectors per modality and payload indexes on high-cardinality, frequently-filtered fields.

• Use payload indexes for fields that appear in most filters to keep ANN queries fast.
• Tune ef and top-k together; increase ef when filters shrink the candidate pool to sustain recall.
• Model multiple modalities with named vectors and apply server-side filters for precise, low-latency retrieval.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand how Qdrant combines fast vector search with powerful payload filtering and how to model and tune for production workloads.

body.en:
**In this lesson you will learn:**

- 1) Why hybrid retrieval that blends BM25 (lexical) and vector (semantic) search improves both precision and recall.
- 2) How to fuse ranked lists with robust methods like Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) and score normalization.
- 3) How to apply neural re-ranking (cross-encoders) to top-k candidates to boost final answer quality within tight latency budgets.

Lexical (BM25) search excels at exact term matching, handling acronyms, numbers, and rare keywords, while dense vector search captures semantic similarity and paraphrases. Hybrid retrieval combines both to reduce false negatives (missed relevant items) and false positives. A common pipeline is: (1) Retrieve top-n_bm25 via BM25 and top-n_vec via ANN; (2) Merge and deduplicate candidates; (3) Fuse rankings using a method robust to score scale differences such as Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), or apply calibrated score normalization and weighted sum; (4) Optionally apply a neural cross-encoder re-ranker over the top-r fused candidates to maximize precision@k.

Key design choices include selecting candidate pool sizes (n_bm25, n_vec), choosing a fusion strategy (RRF is simple and strong), and setting r (re-rank depth) based on latency and model cost. Re-ranking models (e.g., cross-encoders from open-source or hosted APIs) score query–document pairs directly, typically improving ordering within the top results. Guardrails include consistent text preprocessing across indices, lightweight deduplication, and careful score handling (since BM25 and vector scores are not commensurate without normalization). Evaluate with recall@k and nDCG; tune candidate sizes and fusion weights to maximize downstream task quality while meeting SLOs.

• Complementarity: BM25 captures exact terms; vectors capture semantics—together they raise recall and precision.
• Fusion: Use Reciprocal Rank Fusion or normalized weighted fusion to combine ranked lists reliably.
• Re-ranking: A cross-encoder applied to the fused top-k often yields the biggest gains in precision@k.

• Hybrid retrieval combines BM25 and vectors to balance exact matching and semantic understanding.
• Use RRF (or careful normalization) to fuse rankings from heterogeneous scorers.
• Apply cross-encoder re-ranking on a small fused pool to maximize precision within latency and cost budgets.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You can now design and tune a hybrid retrieval pipeline that fuses BM25 with vector search and uses neural re-ranking for high-quality results.

A grounded prompt template is the contract between your retrieval pipeline and the language model.

Chain-of-thought variants ask the model to cite evidence before stating a conclusion, reducing hallucination rates.

Template versioning and A/B testing are essential because small wording changes can dramatically shift faithfulness metrics such as RAGAS AnswerFaithfulness and ContextPrecision.

Citations close the trust loop between an AI answer and its documentary evidence.

The pipeline starts in the prompt: each retrieved chunk is labeled with a reference token such as [1] or [DOC:invoice_policy_v2].

The LLM is instructed to embed these tokens inline as it writes.

Post-generation, a parser extracts the tokens, deduplicates them, and maps each to a metadata record containing title, URL or file path, page number, and confidence score.

On the frontend, tokens render as superscript links or hover cards that display a snippet of the source chunk.

Design principles include progressive disclosure (show a compact badge first, expand on click), confidence banding (color or icon indicating retrieval score), and always providing a 'View full document' affordance.

In a production RAG system serving multiple user roles or tenants, every retrieved chunk must be authorised for the requesting identity. The architecture layers access control at ingestion and retrieval.

During ingestion, each document chunk's metadata is enriched with an ACL field—a list of user IDs, group IDs, or role names permitted to read it. At query time, the retrieval layer applies a metadata pre-filter so only chunks whose ACL includes the caller's identity are candidates for ANN search.

This filter must be applied before—not after—ranking to prevent leaking chunk content through relevance scores. Identity context flows from the API gateway via JWT claims or OAuth 2.0 scopes into the retrieval service.

A dedicated ACL resolver normalises group memberships and role expansions before constructing the filter. Row-level security in relational metadata stores (e.g., PostgreSQL RLS) can complement vector-store filters for hybrid architectures.

question.en: Why must ACL pre-filters be applied before approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) ranking rather than after?

text.en: Post-ranking filters are computationally more expensive
Applying filters after ranking could expose unauthorised chunk content through relevance scores, creating a side-channel leak
Vector stores do not support filtering after ranking
Pre-filters improve embedding quality for authorised documents

explanation.en: If ACL filtering is applied post-ranking, the similarity scores of unauthorised chunks have already been computed and could indirectly reveal information about their content. Pre-filtering ensures unauthorised chunks are never considered during the search at all.

It generates embeddings for user queries based on their role

explanation.en: An ACL resolver translates hierarchical roles and group memberships into the flat set of identifiers needed to build the vector-store metadata filter. title.en: Production Refresh, Jobs, Monitoring and Rollback

body.en:
A production RAG service degrades if its vector index drifts from the underlying knowledge base. Refresh pipelines solve this by re-ingesting changed documents on a schedule or event trigger.

Incremental refresh detects document additions, updates, and deletions via change-data-capture (CDC) events or timestamp comparisons, re-embeds only affected chunks, and upserts them into the index—minimising compute cost. Full refresh rebuilds the entire index from scratch and is used for embedding model upgrades or major schema changes.

Orchestration tools such as Apache Airflow, Prefect, or Dagster schedule jobs, manage retries, and send alerts on failure. Observability requires three layers: infrastructure metrics (job duration, CPU/memory), retrieval metrics (recall@k, MRR tracked via a golden query set), and answer quality metrics (faithfulness, answer relevancy sampled daily).

Index versioning—maintaining a 'blue' live index and a 'green' candidate index—enables zero-downtime refreshes and instant rollback by re-pointing the query router to the previous version if quality metrics degrade. Canary rollouts let a small traffic percentage hit the new index before full promotion.

• Blue/green index versioning: Maintaining two index versions simultaneously—a live 'blue' index serving production traffic and a 'green' candidate—allowing atomic traffic cutover and instant rollback.

question.en: What is the primary advantage of incremental refresh over full index rebuild?

text.en: Incremental refresh produces higher-quality embeddings for unchanged documents
It reduces compute and time cost by re-processing only documents that have changed since the last refresh
It eliminates the need for an orchestration tool like Airflow
It allows the vector store to automatically detect embedding model upgrades

explanation.en: Incremental refresh processes only the delta of changed documents (adds, updates, deletes), making it far cheaper in compute and faster to complete than rebuilding the entire index, which is reserved for scenarios like embedding model upgrades.

question.en: In a blue/green index versioning strategy, what triggers a rollback to the blue (previous) index?

text.en: The green index finishes building successfully
A scheduled maintenance window occurs
Quality metrics such as faithfulness or recall on the golden query set degrade below an acceptable threshold after the green index is promoted
The number of documents in the green index exceeds that of the blue index

explanation.en: Rollback is triggered when post-promotion monitoring detects that the new (green) index causes retrieval recall, faithfulness, or other quality metrics to fall below defined thresholds. The query router is then re-pointed to the stable blue index with no downtime.

question.en: Which observability layer specifically measures whether the knowledge base refresh has maintained or improved answer quality?

text.en: Infrastructure metrics (job duration, CPU usage)
Network throughput metrics from the API gateway
Answer quality metrics such as faithfulness and answer relevancy sampled against a golden query set
Token usage metrics from the LLM API billing dashboard

explanation.en: Answer quality metrics (faithfulness, answer relevancy) evaluated against a fixed golden query set are the definitive signal for whether a refresh has maintained knowledge quality. Infrastructure metrics tell you if the job ran; answer quality metrics tell you if it ran correctly.
